parrafos: Because of the number of different languages in the European Union, there are different, unofficial, names for this unit (the French call them "centimes" and the Spanish "céntimos", for example).

It was created in 1999, but until 1 January 2002 it was used only for electronic payments. In 2002, 12 countries of the European Union (EU) took their state currencies out of circulation and adopted euro notes and coins as their only money. There was a change-over period, called the "transition period", when both the old national money and the euro were accepted, but by 1 March 2002, all 12 countries were using just euros.

In 2007, Slovenia became the 13th country to use the euro. In 2008 Cyprus and Malta became the 14th and 15th countries to use the euro. In 2009, Slovakia became the 16th country to use the euro. In 2011, Estonia became the 17th country to use the euro. In 2014, Latvia became the 18th country and in 2015, Lithuania became the 19th country to use the euro. In 2023, Croatia became the 20th country to use the euro. In 2026, Bulgaria became the 21st country to use the euro.
There are seven different banknotes, each one with a different colour, size and face value: €5 (grey), €10 (red), €20 (blue), €50 (orange), €100 (green), €200 (yellow), €500 (purple).

On every banknote, there is a picture of a different European building style. All banknotes are the same throughout the entire eurozone; there are no different designs for different countries, unlike the euro coins. One side of each coin is the same in all euro countries. The other side is different since each country who mints the coins inserts a symbol relating to that country. Today there are many different sets of coins. Any of the coins can be used everywhere throughout the eurozone despite the country-specific symbol on the back.
The ten new European countries that entered the European Union in May 2004 are planning to adopt the Euro also. First they must meet some conditions to show that they have stable economies.
resumen_es: Reviews the creation of the euro (1999 and 2002), the successive entry of countries up to Bulgaria in 2026, and what its banknotes and coins look like.

ideas_clave.idea: Owing to the variety of languages in the EU, the hundredth part of the euro is known by several unofficial names.
Introduced in 1999 only for electronic transactions, the euro replaced the national currencies of twelve EU countries in 2002, after a brief period in which both were accepted.
The euro area has expanded step by step, from Slovenia in 2007 to Bulgaria, its twenty-first member, in 2026.
There are seven denominations of banknotes, from five to five hundred euros, each with its own colour and size.
Banknotes, which depict European architectural styles, are identical everywhere, whereas coins carry a national symbol on one side yet remain valid throughout the euro area.
The states that entered the EU in 2004 intend to adopt the euro once they prove that their economies are stable.

resumen_modelo: The text outlines the history and features of the euro. Launched in 1999 for electronic payments only, it replaced the national currencies of twelve EU countries in 2002, after a brief transition period. The euro area has since expanded gradually, reaching twenty-one members with Bulgaria in 2026. While its seven banknotes, decorated with European architectural styles, are identical everywhere, coins combine a common side with a national one, yet remain valid throughout the eurozone. Finally, the states that joined the EU in 2004 must prove their economic stability before adopting it.

preguntas.cita: It was created in 1999, but until 1 January 2002 it was used only for electronic payments.

preguntas.explicacion: Croatia was the twentieth (2023). Bulgaria was the twenty-first (2026), Lithuania the nineteenth (2015) and Slovakia the sixteenth (2009).

respuestas: One side of each coin is identical in all euro countries, while the other side bears a symbol chosen by the issuing country; nevertheless, every coin can be used throughout the eurozone.
